serpGaps: No ranking page ties the redesign scope to a specific lifecycle metric: they list generic 'signs you need a redesign' (outdated look, complaints) instead of 'trial accounts stall before the first value moment -> flow fix on onboarding'.
Scope options (refresh / overhaul / rebuild) are described in prose but nobody gives a decision path a buyer can walk with their own data, or says what each tier means in weeks and budget.

B2B SaaS has a second at-risk group that generic guides ignore: workspace admins who configured roles, saved views and integrations for their whole team. A redesign that breaks their setup multiplies churn risk per account.

Pages say 'test on a small cohort' but do not separate testing with existing power users (change aversion, speed on familiar tasks) from new trial users (learnability). Those two tests answer different questions.
Nobody defines rollback thresholds before launch or shows a rollout ramp with gates (which metric must hold before the next step).

Change aversion is mentioned as a vibe; few cite the original Google/GV writing on it or explain how to tell temporary aversion from a worse design (track task success and return usage over weeks, not day-1 sentiment).
Generic product-redesign pages (eleken) are not SaaS-specific: no trial-to-paid, renewal timing, plan/billing screens or account-level settings.
Unsourced uplift numbers are common ('improve activation by 40%', '20-30% lift in activation within the first month'): our post wins on honesty by using only our case-study facts and named sources.

outline.h2: What is a SaaS product redesign, and what is it not?
outline.answerHint: A SaaS product redesign changes the flows, structure and screens that decide a subscription metric (activation, retention, upgrades); a new colour palette on the same flows is a UI refresh, not a redesign.
points: Myth intro sets up this section: 'the product looks dated, so we need a redesign'. Counter it in 2-3 sentences: users churn because of flows, not fonts.
Define the 3 layers a redesign can touch: visual layer, flow/structure layer, platform/architecture layer.
Early UP link to the hub with anchor 'SaaS UX design' (or 'SaaS UX design services').
One sentence on why SaaS differs from a one-off app redesign: every change lands on paying users mid-subscription.

outline.h2: Which metrics tell you a SaaS redesign is due?
outline.answerHint: Redesign when a lifecycle metric stalls for reasons users can show you: trial accounts that never reach the first value moment, weekly active use that drops after month 1, flat upgrades, or support tickets about setup and navigation.
points: Map each lifecycle stage to its trigger metric and the evidence that proves the cause is UX (funnel step in Amplitude/Mixpanel, session recordings, ticket tags, churn-survey reasons). Present as an HTML table, not an image.
Use the Google HEART framework (cite the 2010 CHI paper) to pick 1 goal-signal-metric per stage; do not re-explain HEART at length (the hub mentions it).

DOWN link: ToolsGroup case study (75% of sales losses traced to UI, not features; 30+ stakeholder interviews) as proof that the cause can be UX rather than missing features. Use only figures in the case-study file.
Counter-signal: when the metric drop is pricing, positioning or a missing integration, a redesign will not fix it.

outline.h2: Flow fix, lifecycle redesign or platform rebuild: which scope fits?
outline.answerHint: Pick the smallest scope that addresses the stalled metric: a flow fix for 1 broken journey, a lifecycle redesign when several stages leak, a platform rebuild only when navigation, roles and components cannot hold the product any more.
points: Visual: decision tree (see visuals[0]). The prose walks one path; the image shows all branches.

Comparison table of the 3 tiers: what changes, who is affected, typical duration. Durations and prices come only from the hub: 4-8 weeks for onboarding/lifecycle work at $25,000-$60,000; 8-16 weeks and $60,000-$180,000 when a component library/design system is needed. Mention once, then link to the hub section /services/saas-ux-design/#how-much-does-saas-ux-design-cost. Do not turn this into a cost guide.
Note: a front-end rebuild and a redesign are separate decisions; coupling them doubles launch risk (expand in FAQ).
Natural invitation: 'we run the scoping as the discovery step of a 4-8 week sprint'.

outline.h2: How do you set a baseline before anyone opens Figma?
outline.answerHint: Record the current numbers for the 3-5 flows in scope, the success threshold and the rollback threshold, and interview 5-8 customers, before design starts; without a baseline nobody can prove the redesign worked.
points: Baseline sheet fields: flow, current completion rate, time on task, related ticket volume, target, rollback trigger. Keep it a list in the post (no image).
Check that events are instrumented; a redesign that renames screens breaks old funnels, so map old event names to new ones before launch.
Jobs to be Done interviews with 5-8 customers (hub process) to separate the job from the current UI.
First-hand angle: what we ask for in week 1 (analytics read access, ticket export, churn-survey text, list of top accounts by seat count).

outline.h2: Which users does a redesign put at risk?
outline.answerHint: Three groups carry the risk: power users whose muscle memory breaks, workspace admins who configured the product for their whole team, and accounts close to renewal.
points: Visual: 2x2 framework (see visuals[1]) of usage frequency vs size of change, showing where to protect, where to test hardest, where to move fast.

Change aversion: cite Aaron Sedley's GV Library article and the NN/g 'Users hate change' video; explain that day-1 complaints are expected and the signal is whether task success and return usage recover over the following weeks.

B2B specifics: preserve saved views, keyboard shortcuts, custom fields and role settings through migration; give admins notice before end users. Link to /industries/saas/ for admin and permission design (industry page, not a different hub).
Renewal timing: avoid forcing the new UI on accounts in their renewal window.

outline.h2: How do you test a redesigned flow with existing users and new trials?
outline.answerHint: Run two tests: existing users complete their weekly tasks in old and new versions (speed and errors), and people new to the product attempt onboarding in the new version only (learnability).
points: 5 participants per round per group, prototype in Maze (hub process); cite NN/g 5-user article for the round size.
Score each round with the System Usability Scale (SUS); compare old vs new for existing users. Cite the usability.gov / Brooke SUS source.
What to do when power users are slower on day 1 but new users succeed: plan a transition aid, do not roll back the design.
Single allowed cross-hub link: /services/usability-testing-services/ with anchor 'usability testing services' in this section only.

outline.h2: How do you roll out a SaaS redesign without a churn spike?
outline.answerHint: Ship in gated steps: internal use, opt-in beta with a switch back to the old UI, a percentage rollout behind a feature flag, then a dated sunset of the old UI, moving to the next step only when baseline metrics hold.
points: Numbered steps with a gate per step (which metric must hold, for how long).
Visual: rollout ramp with gates and rollback loops (see visuals[2]).
Feature-flag percentage rollouts: cite LaunchDarkly's soft-launch article. Do not invent percentages as industry norms; any ramp numbers are labelled as an example.
Communication: admin email first, in-app notice, changelog entry, help-centre updates; say why the change helps the user's job.
Old-UI toggle: offer it for a fixed window with a published sunset date; collect a reason when users switch back.

outline.h2: Which redesign mistakes turn into churn?
outline.answerHint: The costly mistakes are redesigning every screen at once, launching without a baseline, removing the old UI on day 1, breaking admin configurations, and shipping a new design system before the flows are fixed.
points: 5-6 mistakes, each with the cheaper alternative (bullet list, not a table, to vary list style).
Redesign driven by a rebrand or a new design system rather than a stalled metric.
Moving navigation and core workflows in the same release.
Silently renaming objects users search for.
Leaving help docs, screenshots and onboarding emails on the old UI.

outline.h2: What should you measure in the first 30 days after launch?
outline.answerHint: Compare the redesigned flows against the baseline every week for 30 days: completion rate, time on task, related ticket volume, switch-back rate to the old UI and, for onboarding, activation of new trial accounts.
points: Visual: before/after flow map (see visuals[3]) showing a multi-screen path collapsed into fewer steps.

DOWN links: Apex HCM (200+ screens reduced to 6 steps in enterprise payroll; VP Product quote 'The new flow cut onboarding time by more than half.') and TradeZella (+40% user interaction, +25% retention, +30% new customers after a dashboard and onboarding revamp; the challenge list includes 'no onboarding guide'). Use only facts in the case-study files and attribute the quote.
When to iterate vs roll back, based on the thresholds set in the baseline section.
Lead moment (see leadAngle) and the second UP link to the hub near the end, anchor e.g. 'our SaaS UX design sprint' pointing to /services/saas-ux-design/.

faqs.q: How long does a SaaS product redesign take?
faqs.hint: Flow or lifecycle redesign: 4-8 weeks (hub). With a design system: 8-16 weeks (hub). Rollout adds weeks on top; say so without inventing a number.

faqs.q: Should you let users switch back to the old UI?
faqs.hint: Yes, for a fixed, announced window during the beta; the switch-back rate and reasons are a key signal. Remove it on the published sunset date.

faqs.q: Should you rebuild the front end and redesign at the same time?
faqs.hint: No, in most cases: separate the decisions so bugs and design changes are not confused in metrics. Exception: when the old front end cannot render the new flows at all.

faqs.q: Do you need a design system before a SaaS redesign?
faqs.hint: No. Fix the flows first; extract components from the redesigned screens. A design system becomes part of scope at platform-rebuild tier (hub: $60,000-$180,000, 8-16 weeks).

faqs.q: How do you announce a SaaS redesign to customers?
faqs.hint: Admins first, then in-app notice and changelog; lead with the job it makes easier, include what moved where and the old-UI sunset date.
